NUEVO LAREDO, Tamaulipas — The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned Nuevo Laredo businessman Gamaliel Garza and nine of his businesses, accusing them of providing or attempting to provide financial, technological, and material support to the Cártel del Noreste, according to a report by Ahora MX published Thursday.

The Cártel del Noreste is one of seven Mexican criminal organizations the United States has designated as terrorist organizations.

Garza’s son, Gamaliel Garza Elías, was also accused of channeling funds toward the campaigns of political candidates favored by the cartel, the report states. OFAC further sanctioned Tamex Leasing and Francisco Javier Inzunza Partida, described as a dispatcher for the firm who allegedly managed the shipment of two trailers that were seized for transporting hidden narcotics.

The U.S. report also names Pablo César Guajardo Álvarez, alias “Takia,” as the current plaza boss of the Cártel del Noreste in Nuevo Laredo, previously the organization’s chief of hitmen. Under the sanctions, any property or assets of the designated persons in the United States, or in the possession of U.S. citizens, are frozen and must be reported to OFAC.

The racehorse connection

Among the sanctioned entities is Club La Molienda, a racetrack, restaurant, and bar outside Nuevo Laredo that the U.S. report says is allegedly controlled by the cartel. The venue generates income through entry fees charged to both horse racers and spectators, according to the report.

Cartel leaders allegedly acquire American Quarter Horses — many brought from the United States — to race at La Molienda. The report says the track is controlled by Z-40, Miguel Ángel Treviño Morales, one of the cartel’s founders, though its day-to-day management falls to various leaders and associates of the criminal group.

Treviño Morales was detained in 2013 and is serving a sentence in the United States. He and his brother Omar, the Z-42, have a long history of alleged money laundering through the purchase of racehorses: between 2008 and 2012, they bought and sold racing specimens with drug money, trained them, and raced them in the United States, the report states. Over a 30-month period, frontmen and shell companies tied to Los Zetas — the Cártel del Noreste’s predecessor — spent $16 million in New Mexico, Oklahoma, California, and Texas to sustain the operation, allegedly laundering more than $22 million. In June 2012, U.S. authorities seized 455 horses at an Oklahoma ranch, racetracks, and events.

Sources:

  • Ahora MX: “Cártel del Noreste: El lavadero con caballos de carreras” (Oct. 22, 2026)

excerpt: OFAC says Gamaliel Garza and nine Nuevo Laredo businesses allegedly supported the Cártel del Noreste; sanctions also hit Club La Molienda, a racetrack the U.S. says generates cartel income through American Quarter Horse racing.
title: U.S. Treasury sanctions Nuevo Laredo businessman, nine firms over alleged Cártel del Noreste ties
